h1: Women in Indian brewing: getting in and getting on
title: Women in Indian Brewing | Craft Beer School
desc: Practical advice for women starting and building a brewing career in India: routes in, the physical side, safety, mentors and how to grow.
teaser: Brewing in India has deep roots in women's hands. Here is practical advice for women building a career in it today.
standfirst: Women have brewed for as long as anyone has. In a modern Indian brewery the work, the skills and the routes in are the same for everyone, though some practical questions come up more often for women. We answer them plainly.
sections:
In many parts of India, traditional rice beers have long been brewed by women at home. In the North-East, drinks such as apong in Assam and zutho in Nagaland come from household traditions where women hold the knowledge of starter cultures and fermentation. Brewing as women's work is far older than the modern brewery.

Commercial brewing in India grew up later and mostly in factories. Its production floors have historically been staffed largely by men. That is changing as craft breweries, labs and brewpubs open. The routes in are open to anyone with the skills.

The usual paths apply. Science graduates in microbiology, biotechnology, food technology or chemistry often start in quality control. Others start in the cellar, on packaging or through an internship at a brewpub. Our guide to becoming a brewer in India sets out the steps. Our guide to a career in brewery quality control covers the lab route.

Taproom, sales and sensory roles are also strong entry points and they lead into brewing more often than people assume.

Brewing is physical work for everyone. A full 50 litre steel keg weighs roughly 60 kg. Malt usually arrives in 25 kg or 50 kg sacks. No one should be lifting those badly, whoever they are.

Good breweries use trolleys, keg lifters, hoists and two-person lifts. Learn proper lifting technique, ask for the right equipment and do not feel you have to prove anything by lifting alone. Technique and the right kit matter far more than raw strength.

Ask about practical things at interview: shift timings, transport for late finishes, changing facilities and properly fitting safety gear. Boots and gloves sized for women are not always stocked, so raise it early.

Indian law requires employers above a certain size to have an internal committee for complaints of sexual harassment. It is reasonable to ask how a brewery handles concerns. A good employer will answer without hesitation.

Find people who will answer questions and vouch for you. Head brewers, QC managers and senior brewers are often generous with time when approached directly. Industry events, tasting groups and online brewing communities are good places to meet them.

The Pink Boots Society is an international organisation that supports women in brewing and the wider fermented drinks trade through education and networking. Check whether there is an active group near you or join its online events.

Be a mentor as well as finding one. Once you have a year or two of experience, answer the questions of people just starting. Brewing in India is a small world and the people you help early often become colleagues, employers or collaborators later.

Some women report being assumed to be in sales or front of house when they walk onto a brewery floor. The simplest response is often to keep doing the technical work visibly and well. Ask precise questions, record your numbers and speak up when something looks wrong in a tank. Competence on the floor is noticed quickly.

If something crosses a line, write down what happened and when, then use the channels the employer has set up. Talk to someone you trust in the industry for advice. You should not have to put up with harassment to keep a brewing job.

Equally, many brewery teams are welcoming and glad of anyone who works hard and learns fast. Look for those teams. Ask current or former staff what it is like to work there before you accept an offer.

Progress in brewing comes from technical depth that nobody can argue with: understanding fermentation, hygiene, quality and process control well enough to explain any decision with evidence. That is where a solid grounding pays off. Many people who feel overlooked on a brewery floor find their footing once they can read a fermentation log better than anyone else in the room.

Professional exams, tasting qualifications and documented results all build a record that speaks for itself. Keep yours.
faqs: Is brewing a good career for women in India?
Yes. The skills and routes in are the same for everyone. Quality, lab, sensory and production roles are all open to women.
Do I need to be very strong to work in a brewery?
No. Lifting technique and equipment such as trolleys and keg lifters matter more than strength. Good breweries use them for everyone.
Are there networks for women in brewing?
The Pink Boots Society is one international network. Local tasting groups, industry events and online brewing communities are also useful.
